interactive.title: Mean and RMS from the area
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens on the mean and RMS values of a changing current. Each screen has a graph of current in amps against time, drawn from a rule the screen names, with bars or a flat rectangle laid over it. The first screen takes lesson 8's current, i = 3t² from 0 s to 2 s, whose area is 8 C: a flat rectangle 4 A high over the same 2 s has the same area, because 8 ÷ 2 = 4, and the part of the curve above it fills the gap below it. Then an a.c. current, a sine wave drawn by the page with a peak of 10 A: over a whole cycle the bars below the axis are hatched and count as minus, and the mean readout shows 0 A. Over half a cycle a slider sets how many bars, from 4 to 100, each as tall as the current at its middle, and the mean of their heights goes 6.53, 6.41, then 6.37 A, 0.637 of the peak. Then the squared current is drawn under the current. A ramp, i = 3t rising to 6 A in 2 s, has a square, 9t², rising to 36 A²; its mean, 12 A², is a flat band, and a readout takes its square root, 3.46 A. On the sine wave's screen the square runs between 0 and 100 A²; a slider marked Fold lifts each hump above the 50 A² line, moves it a quarter cycle along, turns it upside down and drops it into the dip there, where it fits exactly, leaving a flat band at 50 A², whose root is 7.07 A. It fits because a quarter cycle on, the squared current is always 100 minus what it is now: a sine wave is the height of a point going steadily round a circle of radius 10, a quarter turn later its height is what its sideways distance was, and by Pythagoras height² + sideways distance² = 100. A later screen sets three waves side by side, half a cycle of a square wave and of a sine wave, and a ramp, each with its mean, its RMS value and their ratio, the form factor. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it: a puzzle offers three answers, and a wrong pick is shown going wrong on the graph.
interactive.ignores: The waves are drawn exactly from rules: a perfect sine wave computed by the page, and a ramp that drops back to zero at once. Real a.c. is only close to a sine wave, and a real ramp takes a moment to drop back. Time is stretched so one cycle fills the screen. The heating rule I²R takes the heater's resistance as steady, though a real element's resistance changes a little as it warms.

explain.text:
The mean value of a graph over a stretch is the area under it divided by the stretch's length: the height of the flat rectangle with the same area.[^5] The RMS value says how big a changing current is for heating: square the graph, take the mean of the square, then take the square root.[^6] For a sine wave that comes to the peak ÷ √2,[^7] and you can see why without any trigonometry.

Remember the current i = 3t² amps from 0 s to 2 s in lesson 8: the area under it, the charge, is 8 C. A steady current moving the same 8 C in the same 2 s would be 8 ÷ 2 = 4 A, a flat rectangle 4 A high and 2 s long with the same area. That height is the [[mean value]], the definite integral divided by the length of the stretch,[^5] the same move as the mean effective pressure in the last lesson. Where the curve rises above the rectangle, the extra area exactly makes up for where it sits below, because the two shapes hold the same 8 C. The mean is not the average of the end values, (0 + 12) ÷ 2 = 6 A, because this curve spends most of the 2 s low down and only shoots up near the end; on a straight line the two do agree, which is why the slip is easy to make, but not in general. With equal bars the mean is plain averaging: each bar's area is its height times the same width, so the bars' total area ÷ their total width is the average of their heights.

An a.c. current flows one way, then back. The a.c. from a generator follows the shape of a sine wave,[^8] drawn here with a peak of 10 A; its trigonometry waits for a later course. Over a whole cycle the backward half has the same area as the forward half, and area below the axis counts as minus, so the mean is zero.[^1] A mean of zero says nothing about how big the current is, so for its size the mean is taken over half a cycle, where it flows one way: the bars settle on 6.37 A, 0.637 of the peak.[^2] Heating needs something different again. At each moment a heater takes power i²R, so its heat goes with the square of the current: twice the current gives four times the heat, and a backward current heats just as well, because a minus times a minus is a plus. Over a cycle its mean power is the mean of i² times R. A steady current I gives I²R. The R is the same on both sides, so the two heat alike when I² equals the mean of i²: square the graph, find its mean, then take the square root.[^6] That is the [[RMS value]], short for root mean square: the steady direct current that would give a circuit the same energy.[^9] Take a ramp, i = 3t amps from 0 s to 2 s, rising to 6 A and dropping back. Under it is a triangle, half of 2 s × 6 A, so 6 C, and its mean is 6 C ÷ 2 s = 3 A. Its square is 9t², which the reverse rule turns into 3t³, so its area from 0 s to 2 s is 24 and its mean is 24 ÷ 2 = 12 A². The RMS value is √12 = 3.46 A, more than the mean, because squaring makes the big currents count for more. Any ramp from 0 up to a peak A in a time T works the same way. It is i = A × t ÷ T, its square is A² × t² ÷ T², and the reverse rule turns that into A² × t³ ÷ (3T²), which at T is A² × T ÷ 3. Divide by the length T and the mean square is A² ÷ 3, so the RMS value is A ÷ √3: 6 ÷ 1.732 = 3.46 A.

Now square the sine wave with its 10 A peak. The square runs between 0 and 100 A², never below the axis, and repeats every half cycle, because the backward half squares to the same humps as the forward half. Its humps above 50 A², half the peak squared, are the same shape as its dips below 50 A², turned upside down, so each hump lifts off, moves a quarter cycle along, turns over and drops exactly into the dip there, leaving a flat band at 50 A². One way to picture why: a sine wave is the height of a point going steadily round a circle whose radius is the peak. A quarter turn later its height is what its sideways distance was, and by Pythagoras height² + sideways distance² = 10² = 100 at every moment. So the squared wave and the squared wave a quarter cycle later always add up to 100: wherever one is above 50 by some amount, the other is below 50 by the same amount. The mean of the square is therefore 50 A², and the RMS value is √50 = 7.07 A, the peak ÷ √2, about 0.707 of the peak;[^7][^3] the other way round, the peak is 1.414 × the RMS value.[^4] That is more than the half-cycle mean of 6.37 A, and the RMS value ÷ the mean value is called the [[form factor]]:[^10] 7.07 ÷ 6.37 = 1.11 for a sine wave, and 3.46 ÷ 3 = 1.15 for the ramp. Like the work from a pV diagram, a mean or RMS value comes from an area under a graph, found by bars or the reverse rule, then divided by a length: one more way the integral turns a quantity that keeps changing into a single number you can use. **The mean value is the area under a graph ÷ its length;[^5] the RMS value is the square root of the mean of the squared graph,[^6] which for a sine wave is its peak ÷ √2.[^7]**

analogy.text: Picture raking a heap of spoil flat along a trench. The high spots fill the low spots, and the flat level you end with is the heap's mean height: its side-on area ÷ its length, whatever shape it started. The RMS value is the same levelling done on a heap whose every height has been squared first: rake that flat, then take the square root of its level.
analogy.breaks: Spoil cannot hang below the ground, but a graph's area below the axis counts as minus, which is why an a.c. wave's whole-cycle mean is zero. And spoil packs down as you rake it, while an area moved about on a graph stays exactly the same size.

practice.text:
- Mean value: find the area under the graph over the stretch, by the reverse rule or by bars, and divide by the stretch's length.
- For a.c., take the mean over half a cycle: over a whole cycle it comes to zero.
- RMS value: square the graph, find the mean of the square, take the square root. Square first, root last.
- From readings only: split the stretch into equal strips, read the value at each strip's middle, square each reading, average the squares, then take the root.
- Sine wave: RMS = peak × 0.707, peak = RMS × 1.414, half-cycle mean = peak × 0.637.
- A ramp rising steadily from 0 to its peak and dropping back: mean = peak ÷ 2, RMS = peak ÷ √3.
- Form factor = RMS value ÷ mean value.[^10]

**Rules of thumb:** for the waves in this lesson the RMS value lies at or between the half-cycle mean and the peak. The 0.707 is the sine wave's figure; other shapes usually give other figures, so for them square, mean and root.

**Worked example:** Say a sine current peaks at 15 A. Its RMS value is 15 × 0.707 = 10.6 A, its half-cycle mean is 15 × 0.637 = 9.56 A, and its form factor is 10.6 ÷ 9.56 = 1.11.

**Worked example from readings:** Say half a cycle of an odd-shaped current is split into four equal strips, with middle readings of 2, 6, 6 and 2 A. The mean is 16 ÷ 4 = 4 A. The squares are 4, 36, 36 and 4, so the mean square is 80 ÷ 4 = 20 A² and the RMS value is √20 = 4.47 A. The form factor is 4.47 ÷ 4 = 1.12.

**Where you will meet it:** the MCA's Marine Electro-technology syllabus asks for the mean value, RMS value and form factor of sine waves and of other wave shapes,[^11] and an HN engineering maths unit applies integration to mean values and root mean square values.[^12]

**Common mistakes**
- Taking the average of the end values as the mean: it is right on a straight line, but not in general.
- Taking an a.c. mean over a whole cycle and getting zero.
- Using the mean as the RMS value.
- Forgetting the square root, which leaves an answer in A².
- Dividing the peak by 2 instead of by √2.
- Using peak ÷ √2 for a wave that is not a sine wave.
- Dividing an RMS value by 1.414 to get the peak, instead of multiplying.

interactive.html:
Graphs of a changing current against time, each drawn from a rule, with bars or a flat rectangle laid over them.

Each wave is drawn from its rule with example values; each mean and RMS is worked out from it.

checks.label: The average value of a function on an interval is its definite integral divided by the interval’s length: each flat rectangle drawn has the curve’s area over the same stretch, 4 A × 2 s = 8 C under 3t², 3 A × 3 s = 9 C under t², 3 A × 2 s = 6 C under the ramp and 12 A² × 2 s = 24 under its square

The average of a whole cycle is zero: on the a.c. screen the hatched bars below the axis cancel the bars above at every bar count from 4 to 100, so their heights add up to 0 A, and the sine wave’s area over a whole cycle comes to 0

Using only half a cycle the average value is 0.637 of the peak value: for the 10 A peak the bars’ mean drawn goes 6.53, 6.41 and 6.37 A for 4, 8 and 100 bars, falling with every extra bar towards 0.637 of the peak, and the 20 A puzzle’s answer is 0.637 × 20 = 12.7 A

To find the RMS value of any function, square it, find the mean over the period, then take the square root: the ramp to 6 A gives √12 = 3.46 A, the ramp to 12 A gives √48 = 6.93 A and the 30 V sawtooth 17.3 V, each from 20,000 squared bars, and the RMS level drawn sits at that height

The RMS value of a sine wave is 0.707 of the peak value: the squared 10 A sine wave averages 50 A² over a cycle, the fold leaves its flat band at 50 A², √50 = 7.07 A and 7.07 ÷ 10 = 0.707; the RMS level drawn on the fold screen sits at 7.07 A

The RMS value of a voltage or current is the peak value divided by the square root of 2: 10 ÷ √2 = 7.07 A for the 10 A sine wave, and 100 ÷ √2 = 70.7 V in the voltage puzzle, where the RMS level drawn once it is answered sits at 70.7 V

The peak value of a sine wave is equal to 1.414 × the RMS value: an RMS of 5 A gives a peak of 5 × 1.414 = 7.07 A, the wave drawn once the puzzle is answered, and that wave’s own RMS from 20,000 squared bars is 5 A

The RMS value is the steady current that would provide the same energy: squared, the steady 7.07 A drawn on the fold screen matches the 50 A² mean of the squared sine wave, and the steady 3.46 A on the ramp screen matches the 12 A² mean of its square, so with the same resistance each heats alike

Calculates the rms value, mean value and form factor of sinusoidal and non-sinusoidal wave forms: the three-wave screen shows the square wave 10 A, 10 A and 1, the sine wave 6.37 A, 7.07 A and 1.11, and the ramp 3 A, 3.46 A and 1.15, each worked out from its wave by 20,000 bars with the means over half a cycle for the two a.c. waves; the 12 A ramp’s form factor is 6.93 ÷ 6 = 1.15

The fold fits exactly: a quarter cycle on, the squared current is always 100 minus what it is now; folded flat, every point of each hump lands on the curve of the dip it drops into with its flat side on 50 A², the humps fill every dip across the cycle, and each hump keeps its area
Every puzzle offers three different answers and accepts only the right one; each answer’s number is the value its slip gives, rounded as shown

Before Check no puzzle gives its verdict: nothing red and the working ends in a question mark; a picked answer only marks its own value; a right answer draws the answer with nothing red; every wrong answer shows its slip in red
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 5 s of its screen opening, and every pick’s or answer’s motion within 1.3 s

applied.problem: The closing link says a mean or RMS value 'is an area under a graph ... divided by a length', but the RMS value is the square root of the squared graph's area ÷ length, so the sentence is false for RMS as worded.

It gives the ramp a 'half-cycle mean', but the ramp's 3 A mean (used for its 1.15 form factor) is over its whole 2 s rise; over half of that it would be 1.5 A. Only the two a.c. waves take a half-cycle mean.
